One year ago, a giant group of researchers split up into five different groups. Those five groups each focused on one method for improving crop yield from farming. The year has come and gone, and the five groups have come back together, to pool all their data. They will work together for the next year, finding the most efficient, eco-friendly, and most product-gaining techniques. These are the following results the five teams have come up with:

Farming Tower Design Optimization: Team 1 has decided that a hybrid of vertical racks and pyramids, would be the most efficient build for planting, wiring, pumping, and harvesting. They believe that the Pyrack allows for better growing conditions for the plants. Estimated product multiplier: 3x

Structural Design and Stability: Team 2 went all out in designing the building to be unique, but also spacious and functional. The buildings are to look and be similar to these skyscrapers, but have a generally hollow inside, minus the flooring for the farms, and any maintenance rooms. They worked out insulation, and making the building airtight, with entrances and exits have airlocks, to prevent any change in atmosphere. The windows will be fitted with panels that are closed during the day, but are open at night. Estimated product multiplier: 1x

Water Pumping and Perfectness: Team 3 focused on water, and found out that distilled water was deemed the best choice, as it is pure H2O, and lacks any unwanted elements. The team worked on plans for distillation plants that would be built for the towers, and connected straight to the towers' pumping system. Estimated product multiplier: 1x

Lighting and Solar Rays: Team 4 found that 18 hours of light, and 6 hours of darkness was best for crops. The lights will turn on at 4AM every morning, and turn off at 10PM every night. As for lighting colour, full-spectrum fluorescent bulbs were deemed the best choice, as being less energy-intensive and more efficient than single colour LEDs. Estimated product multiplier: 2x

Indoor Climate and Humidity: Lastly, Team 5 discovered that a temperature fluctuating between 22°C and 28°C (72°F and 82°F), was the best zone to grow crops at. For humidity, a relative humidity of 50% was declared the best for crops. A ventilation system was worked out for each floor, that allows outside CO2 to be pulled in, separated from other gasses, and released to the plants creating a building-only atmosphere with 1200-1500 ppm for CO2. The O2 produced by the plants would then be filtered out, making sure only O2 leaves the building, and no CO2. Estimated product multiplier: 4x
